## We measured 20 outcomes. One gave p = 0.03. {#one-among-twenty .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">The L1 experiment now measures 20 markers</p>
<p class="big">Is p = 0.03 still p = 0.03?</p>
<p class="takeaway fragment">The individual number is unchanged.<br>The opportunity to find a small number has changed.</p>
<p class="fine">Hypothetical expansion of the assay—not a revision of the observed enzyme result, p = 0.090.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 00:51–00:53 (2 minutes).**

**Say:** Ask for an answer before revealing the distinction. The raw p-value still describes its particular test under that test's assumptions. But finding a small result after twenty chances is a different event from a single preselected comparison. State the central question aloud: how many chances did we give ourselves to find something? This is a hypothetical expanded L1 protocol; the original enzyme result has not been changed to 0.03. No correction method is needed yet.

**Conceptual point:** A valid individual p-value and the interpretation of a selected finding across many tests are different questions.

**Likely misconception:** Multiplicity changes the measured raw p-value, or its numerical validity removes the need to consider selection.

**Optional follow-up:** Would your answer change if this marker had been the sole prespecified primary outcome?

**Sources:** Concepts adapted from CONTENT_MAP.md section 9 and review register: AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 78–80, 167–173, 178–184; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 63–70; DoctaMed.pdf p. 44. Figures rebuilt, not copied. Method reference: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/p.adjust.html (Holm strong FWER control; BH FDR and dependence caveats).

:::

## What happens when none of the markers responds? {#twenty-true-nulls .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">Predict before the next experiments appear</p>
<div class="uncertainty-stack">
<img data-fragment-index="0" class="data-plot fragment fade-out" src="figures/generated/multi-twenty-1.png" alt="Twenty raw p-values from simulated experiment 1; all twenty null hypotheses are true." />
<img data-fragment-index="0" class="data-plot fragment fade-in-then-out" src="figures/generated/multi-twenty-2.png" alt="Twenty raw p-values from simulated experiment 2; all twenty null hypotheses are true." />
<img data-fragment-index="1" class="data-plot fragment" src="figures/generated/multi-twenty-3.png" alt="Twenty raw p-values from simulated experiment 3; all twenty null hypotheses are true." />
</div>
<p class="takeaway">Would one value below 0.05 surprise you?</p>
<p class="fine">Six paired changes per marker. Independent markers, all nulls true. First three simulated experiments, unselected.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 00:53–00:56 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** Show one set of twenty p-values and ask for a prediction, then reveal two more experiments. Each marker is tested on six independent normal paired changes with true mean zero and a two-sided paired t procedure. Markers are independent in this illustration; real markers can be correlated. Standardized marker units have SD one, so these are not twenty literal enzyme-activity measurements on one scale. Red dots cross 0.05 and are Type I errors because we know the simulated truth. Ordinary small p-values arise without a biological effect. These are the first three experiments, not chosen to achieve a desired pattern.

**Conceptual point:** A collection of valid individual tests can produce occasional false rejections when all nulls are true.

**Likely misconception:** A p-value below 0.05 cannot arise if the null is true, or red points prove a simulation error.

**Optional follow-up:** What is one repetition here: one marker or a complete experiment with twenty markers?

**Sources:** Concepts adapted from CONTENT_MAP.md section 9 and review register: AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 78–80, 167–173, 178–184; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 63–70; DoctaMed.pdf p. 44. Figures rebuilt, not copied. Method reference: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/p.adjust.html (Holm strong FWER control; BH FDR and dependence caveats).

:::

## How many chances did we give ourselves? {#twenty-chances .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">Predict: how many experiments find at least one?</p>
<div class="fragment" data-fragment-index="0"><img class="data-plot short-plot" src="figures/generated/multi-families.png" alt="First hundred all-null families; crosses indicate at least one raw p below 0.05." /></div>
<p class="takeaway fragment" data-fragment-index="0"><strong>64.27%</strong> of 10,000 experiments found at least one.</p>
<p class="small fragment" data-fragment-index="1">Under independence: 1 − (1 − 0.05)<sup>20</sup> ≈ 0.64</p>
<p class="fine">One symbol = one 20-test experiment. A 5% per-test rate is not a 5% any-error rate.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 00:56–00:59 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** Collect predictions before revealing the grid. Crosses mean at least one of twenty null tests crossed 0.05; the first hundred families are unselected. Across all 10,000, 64.27% had one or more. On the next click show the independence calculation: the probability none crosses is .95 to the twentieth power, so its complement is about .6415. Emphasize that this exact formula requires independent tests with exact .05 marginal size. Correlated valid marker tests do not generally have this same probability. Distinguish the per-test probability from the chance of any false rejection across a family; an expected false count is a third quantity, introduced later.

**Conceptual point:** Many opportunities amplify the probability of at least one Type I error across the collection.

**Likely misconception:** Twenty tests at 5% means a 5% chance of any false finding, or necessarily one error every time.

**Optional follow-up:** Which assumption allowed us to multiply the twenty no-error probabilities?

**Sources:** Concepts adapted from CONTENT_MAP.md section 9 and review register: AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 78–80, 167–173, 178–184; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 63–70; DoctaMed.pdf p. 44. Figures rebuilt, not copied. Method reference: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/p.adjust.html (Holm strong FWER control; BH FDR and dependence caveats).

:::

## Which claims belong to the same family? {#define-family .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">What shared claim would make these one family?</p>
<div class="definitions-pair"><p class="small">20 prespecified cytokines<br>Several treatment contrasts</p><p class="small">Multiple time points<br>Several primary endpoints</p></div>
<p class="medium fragment"><strong>Family-wise error rate (FWER)</strong></p>
<p class="takeaway fragment">Probability of at least one Type I error within a defined family of hypotheses</p>
<p class="fine fragment">The family follows the scientific claims and decision—not whichever results look interesting.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 00:59–01:01 (2 minutes).**

**Say:** Only now name FWER. It is a probability that any true null in a defined family is rejected, even if some other hypotheses in that family are false. Ask which outcomes contribute to the same intended claim or decision. Twenty cytokines for one question may form a family; so might several contrasts, time points or primary endpoints. Scientific context and the promised error protection determine the family; there is not one uniquely correct grouping independent of purpose. Define it prospectively where possible, not after seeing which grouping gives a favorable result.

**Conceptual point:** FWER control requires an interpretable scientific family of claims.

**Likely misconception:** A family is automatically every column in a file, or can be chosen after looking at p-values solely to keep a finding.

**Optional follow-up:** What shared claim would make our twenty L1 markers one family?

**Sources:** Concepts adapted from CONTENT_MAP.md section 9 and review register: AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 78–80, 167–173, 178–184; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 63–70; DoctaMed.pdf p. 44. Figures rebuilt, not copied. Method reference: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/p.adjust.html (Holm strong FWER control; BH FDR and dependence caveats).

:::

## What if we measured 20,000 genes? {#twenty-thousand}

<img class="data-plot short-plot" src="figures/generated/multi-genes.png" alt="Two hundred dots represent twenty thousand genes; ten rust dots represent the expected one thousand raw false positives." />
<p class="takeaway">20,000 × 0.05 = <strong>1,000 expected raw false positives</strong></p>
<p class="fine">All nulls true; valid exact 5% tests. Each dot represents 100 genes. Illustration of an expectation—not one observed screen.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 01:01–01:03 (2 minutes).**

**Say:** Change scale to an exploratory transcriptome-wide screen. Under twenty thousand true nulls, the expected number of raw p-values below .05 is one thousand. Expectation is a repeated-run average, not an exact count in one screen. This expected-count calculation uses linearity of expectation and does not require independent tests if each marginal size is .05; valid conservative tests give at most that expectation. Under independence the probability of at least one is essentially one, a different quantity from the expected count. The dot display depicts the expectation rather than an invented RNA-seq dataset or software output. Protecting against even one error may be demanding for candidate discovery, motivating a different scientific goal.

**Conceptual point:** The expected count of false positives is distinct from the probability of any false positive.

**Likely misconception:** A thousand expected errors means a thousand must occur in this dataset, or it is itself a probability.

**Optional follow-up:** Would a candidate screen and a small set of primary confirmatory outcomes need the same promise?

**Sources:** Concepts adapted from CONTENT_MAP.md section 9 and review register: AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 78–80, 167–173, 178–184; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 63–70; DoctaMed.pdf p. 44. Figures rebuilt, not copied. Method reference: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/p.adjust.html (Holm strong FWER control; BH FDR and dependence caveats).

:::

## What error promise fits a discovery list? {#introduce-fdr}

<p class="small">New simulation: 4 nonzero marker effects + 16 true nulls; independent tests.</p>
<img class="data-plot multi-short" src="figures/generated/multi-fdp.png" alt="False-discovery proportions across the first eighty mixed-truth screens; the mean across ten thousand is about 4.1 percent." />
<p class="takeaway"><strong>FDR:</strong> expected false-discovery proportion over repeated use</p>
<p class="fine">Line: mean false fraction 4.1% across 10,000 screens. No discoveries → fraction 0.<br>One dataset's fraction is not guaranteed to equal the target.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 01:03–01:05 (2 minutes).**

**Say:** Contrast the scientific aim of avoiding even one false confirmatory claim with producing a candidate list for follow-up. Name FDR only after posing the list question. FDR is the expected proportion of false discoveries among all discoveries; if there are no discoveries, the fraction is zero by convention. The first eighty BH-controlled screens show variable realized fractions; the teal line marks the mean across ten thousand, about 4.1%. FDR 5% is not a guarantee about this list — it is a repeated-use expectation. A realized list can have zero, a large fraction, or even all false discoveries. In real science we do not know which specific claims are false. The concept of a fraction rather than a count is the take-home.

**Conceptual point:** FDR is a repeated-procedure expectation of a fraction, not a known fraction in one observed discovery set.

**Likely misconception:** At 5% FDR exactly 5% of this study's significant genes are false.

**Optional follow-up:** Why must a run with no discoveries still have a defined fraction?

**Sources:** Concepts adapted from CONTENT_MAP.md section 9 and review register: AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 78–80, 167–173, 178–184; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 63–70; DoctaMed.pdf p. 44. Figures rebuilt, not copied. Method reference: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/p.adjust.html (Holm strong FWER control; BH FDR and dependence caveats).

:::

## Which promise does the scientific question need? {#fwer-versus-fdr}

<div class="research-paths"><div><h3>Confirmatory family</h3><p class="small">How likely is even one false rejection?<br><strong>FWER</strong></p></div><div><h3>Exploratory candidate list</h3><p class="small">What false fraction is controlled on average?<br><strong>FDR</strong></p></div></div>
<p class="takeaway">Choose the error criterion from the scientific purpose.</p>
<p class="fine">In our mixed simulation, controlling FDR kept the average false fraction at 4.1% — but at least one false hit still occurred in 10.2% of screens.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 01:05–01:07 (2 minutes).**

**Say:** Compare promises rather than declaring a winning correction. A few prespecified primary outcomes may need strong protection against any false claim. A transcriptome-wide candidate screen with independent confirmation planned may prioritize a controlled expected false fraction. In the mixed simulation BH gives FDR 4.13% and FWER 10.16%; those are different denominators and summaries, not contradictory results. These realized rates are model-specific, not guarantees for all datasets. Error control does not establish biological importance; keep magnitude, uncertainty and validation in view.

**Conceptual point:** FWER and FDR address different scientific commitments.

**Likely misconception:** A procedure controlling FDR at 5% must also control the chance of any false rejection at 5%.

**Optional follow-up:** Which promise would you make for a primary claim that determines whether a compound advances?

**Sources:** Concepts adapted from CONTENT_MAP.md section 9 and review register: AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 78–80, 167–173, 178–184; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 63–70; DoctaMed.pdf p. 44. Figures rebuilt, not copied. Method reference: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/p.adjust.html (Holm strong FWER control; BH FDR and dependence caveats).

:::

## You report p = 0.03. What else did you try? {#what-else-tried .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">Name one hidden opportunity from your own work</p>
<div class="multi-choices"><p class="fragment">20 endpoints</p><p class="fragment">Several doses</p><p class="fragment">Several time points</p><p class="fragment">Several subgroups</p><p class="fragment">Different exclusion rules</p><p class="fragment">Transformed or untransformed outcome</p><p class="fragment">Paired or unpaired analysis</p><p class="fragment">One-sided or two-sided test</p><p class="fragment">Stopping or adding observations after a look</p></div>
<p class="takeaway">Multiple opportunities can be visible—or hidden in analytical choices.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 01:07–01:10 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** Reveal the choices one at a time and invite examples. Multiplicity can come from planned parallel tests and from decisions affected by observed outcomes. The opportunities are not interchangeable: paired versus unpaired must follow design; transformations and exclusions can be scientifically justified; stopping rules change the sampling procedure. Do not automatically apply a simple Bonferroni count to every option on this slide. The issue is what full selection process produced the reported analysis and whether its claimed error guarantee accounts for that process. Avoid moralizing: thoughtful analysts can create a data-dependent path without deliberate threshold chasing.

**Conceptual point:** The inferential context includes analytical flexibility, not just the number of outcome columns.

**Likely misconception:** Reporting only one test removes the problem, or every analysis choice can be repaired by counting commands.

**Optional follow-up:** Which choices were fixed by the experimental design, and which could have changed after seeing results?

**Sources:** Concepts adapted from CONTENT_MAP.md section 9 and review register: AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 78–80, 167–173, 178–184; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 63–70; DoctaMed.pdf p. 44. Figures rebuilt, not copied. Method reference: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/p.adjust.html (Holm strong FWER control; BH FDR and dependence caveats).

:::

## The test direction must be specified before seeing the data {#one-sided-after-peeking}

<div class="research-paths">
<div><h3>Planned one-sided</h3><p class="small">Direction fixed before collection: only a reduction is biologically plausible.</p><p class="small">α = 0.05 on one tail. Legitimate.</p></div>
<div><h3>Post-hoc one-sided</h3><p class="small">Direction chosen after seeing the effect is negative: "clearly it's a reduction, so one-sided."</p><p class="small">Two-sided p = 0.090 → one-sided p = 0.045. The α = 0.05 promise was not what was kept.</p></div>
</div>
<p class="takeaway">Choosing the direction after looking is a hidden extra test.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 01:10–01:12 (2 minutes).**

**Say:** The one-sided versus two-sided decision must be made before the data are examined, not after. For the L1 experiment: two-sided p is 0.090. If you look at the data, observe the negative sign, and then decide to use a one-sided test, you obtain p = 0.045 — just across the threshold. But you used the data twice: once to choose the direction, and once to compute the p-value. The effective α is no longer 0.05. The test is legitimate only if the direction was fixed before collection on scientific grounds — for example, if a positive enzyme increase from a kinase inhibitor is mechanistically impossible and would not be reported regardless of size. That constraint must be documented before the experiment. Retrospective justification ("of course we only expected a reduction") is not equivalent.

**Conceptual point:** A p-value guarantees its stated error rate only when the procedure — including the direction — is fully pre-specified. Post-hoc direction choice changes the effective procedure.

**Likely misconception:** Choosing one-sided because the observed direction is "biologically obvious in hindsight" is a legitimate scientific justification.

**Optional follow-up:** How would you document a pre-specified one-sided decision in a lab notebook entry written before the experiment?

**Sources:** Bland & Altman (1994) *BMJ* 309:248 — one-tailed vs two-tailed significance; Vaux (2012) *Nature* 492:180.
:::

## A pause before we examine selection {#multiplicity-break .break-slide}

<p class="big">15-minute break</p>
<p class="takeaway">Next: exploration vs confirmation.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 01:12–01:27 (15 minutes).**

**Say:** Take the scheduled break from 01:12 to 01:27. Resume with exploration versus confirmation. Do not use the break to add teaching content.

**Conceptual point:** Preserve the planned break and attention for the remaining block.

**Likely misconception:** The scheduled break is optional overflow time.

**Optional follow-up:** No audience task during the break.

**Sources:** Concepts adapted from CONTENT_MAP.md section 9 and review register: AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 78–80, 167–173, 178–184; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 63–70; DoctaMed.pdf p. 44. Figures rebuilt, not copied. Method reference: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/p.adjust.html (Holm strong FWER control; BH FDR and dependence caveats).

:::

## Exploration is useful science {#explore-then-confirm .key-message}

<p class="key-label">Key message</p>

<p class="medium">Explore → generate a hypothesis<br>→ independently test it</p>
<p class="key-statement compact">A p-value from exploratory data means little:<br>the hypothesis came from the same data.</p>
<p class="key-support">Show which ideas emerged from the data — and test them in a new experiment.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 01:27–01:29 (2 minutes).**

**Say:** Reconnect to Session 1. Transformations, subgroup inspection and hypothesis generation are legitimate exploratory work. The problem is attaching confirmatory error guarantees as though the hypothesis and analysis had been fixed before those same observations were examined. Report discovery as discovery and independently test important resulting claims with an appropriate design. Independence means genuinely new information not reused to select the claim; it does not guarantee success. Avoid suggesting that every exploratory calculation needs a mechanical adjustment or that exploration is inferior science. Land the key message: when the hypothesis was suggested by the same data, a p-value from those data has almost no evidential value — it describes how unusual the pattern was that we already selected for being unusual. Show the exploration; reserve testing for the new experiment.

**Conceptual point:** Exploration and confirmation serve complementary roles with different inferential claims.

**Likely misconception:** Trying multiple ideas is intrinsically illegitimate, or relabeling the same analysis makes it independent confirmation.

**Optional follow-up:** What would you carry forward from a promising marker screen into a new experiment?

**Sources:** Concepts adapted from CONTENT_MAP.md section 9 and review register: AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 78–80, 167–173, 178–184; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 63–70; DoctaMed.pdf p. 44. Figures rebuilt, not copied. Method reference: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/p.adjust.html (Holm strong FWER control; BH FDR and dependence caveats).

:::

## What does the reader learn from these two reports? {#selective-reporting .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">Compare reports A and B · 1 minute</p>
<div class="research-paths"><div><h3>Report A</h3><p class="small">"Outcome X was significantly affected, p = 0.03."</p></div><div><h3>Report B</h3><p class="small">"We examined 20 prespecified outcomes. X had raw p = 0.03; the full family, effect estimates, intervals and planned multiplicity analysis are reported."</p></div></div>
<p class="takeaway fragment">Same raw p-value. A different view of how it was found.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 01:29–01:32 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** Allow a minute to compare reports and two to discuss. Imagine twenty measured outcomes, nineteen without a small p and one p=.03. Report A hides that context. Report B tells the reader what the family was and makes the full results available; it must actually provide the named estimates and analysis, not merely claim transparency. If Bonferroni on twenty was the plan, .03 becomes .60; other strategies depend on the specified purpose. Reporting all outcomes does not itself correct invalid inference, but concealing them prevents assessment. Distinguish raw from adjusted p-values and ordinary from multiplicity-aware intervals. Do not describe the nineteen as proof that those markers have no effect.

**Conceptual point:** Transparent reporting of outcomes and selection is necessary for interpreting the reported result.

**Likely misconception:** A selected p=.03 tells the complete story, or a transparency sentence alone repairs the statistical analysis.

**Optional follow-up:** What information in Report B changes your interpretation of the same number?

**Sources:** Concepts adapted from CONTENT_MAP.md section 9 and review register: AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 78–80, 167–173, 178–184; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 63–70; DoctaMed.pdf p. 44. Figures rebuilt, not copied. Method reference: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/p.adjust.html (Holm strong FWER control; BH FDR and dependence caveats).

:::

## What can we decide before the data arrive? {#prevent-before-repair}

<div class="synthesis-grid"><p><span>Purpose</span>Confirmatory or exploratory?</p><p><span>Outcomes</span>Primary, secondary and their families</p><p><span>Comparisons</span>Planned contrasts and time points</p><p><span>Included data</span>Analysis population and exclusion rules</p><p><span>Stopping</span>When is collection complete?</p><p><span>Error promise</span>Multiplicity strategy and analysis</p></div>
<p class="takeaway">Prespecification makes the claim and its error guarantee interpretable.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 01:32–01:34 (2 minutes).**

**Say:** Connect the multiplicity problem to experimental design. Where feasible, record the scientific purpose, primary/secondary outcomes, family, contrasts, analysis population, exclusions, stopping and multiplicity strategy before outcomes guide those choices. This can be a clear lab plan; do not claim that every laboratory experiment requires a formal preregistration. Plans may need justified amendments or exploratory follow-up, which should be disclosed as such. Prespecification does not guarantee a correct model or meaningful question; it makes the target and procedure assessable.

**Conceptual point:** Prospective specification clarifies what procedure and set of claims the reported inference represents.

**Likely misconception:** A preregistration label guarantees validity, or every exploratory decision must be fixed in advance.

**Optional follow-up:** Which two choices would you record before repeating this L1 screen?

**Sources:** Concepts adapted from CONTENT_MAP.md section 9 and review register: AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 78–80, 167–173, 178–184; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 63–70; DoctaMed.pdf p. 44. Figures rebuilt, not copied. Method reference: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/p.adjust.html (Holm strong FWER control; BH FDR and dependence caveats).

:::

## One question to carry forward {#which-test-bridge}

<p class="quote uncertainty-final">Fine. But which statistical test should I actually use for my experiment?</p>

::: notes
**Time: 01:34–01:35 (1 minute).**

**Say:** Read the practical question and stop. Do not introduce tests, a decision tree or the next section. This block establishes the context in which a choice of statistical procedure will later make sense.

**Conceptual point:** The next question follows from design, data structure and inferential purpose.

**Likely misconception:** The present discussion supplies a universal test selector.

**Optional follow-up:** Leave this question unanswered.

**Sources:** Concepts adapted from CONTENT_MAP.md section 9 and review register: AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 78–80, 167–173, 178–184; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 63–70; DoctaMed.pdf p. 44. Figures rebuilt, not copied. Method reference: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/p.adjust.html (Holm strong FWER control; BH FDR and dependence caveats).

:::
